title: Teaching Trade-offs Are Hard to Observe
author: Rod Naquin
summary: Coaching a first-year student teacher who now leads two of his sections independently, the author uses the contrast between her tight, structured 3rd period and looser, more energetic 4th period to argue that instructional coaching typically misses the most important thing about teaching: the trade-offs a teacher makes constantly among competing classroom demands. Drawing on Mary Kennedy's framework of teaching's five persistent problems and, more directly, on Wendy Smith and Marianne Lewis's distinction between a one-time dilemma and a permanent paradox, the piece explains that classroom tensions like participation versus order cannot be solved once and abandoned. It then applies Poole and Van de Ven's four organizational responses to unresolvable paradoxes -- separation by space, separation by time, synthesis, and acceptance -- to classroom coaching, and observes that the student teacher is enacting separation by space unconsciously, as a reaction rather than a chosen strategy. The author argues coaches must therefore observe the same teacher across multiple sections and days rather than relying on single scheduled visits, and offers a specific coaching "talk move" that asks a novice teacher to name which competing demand they were serving in a given moment.
points: A single scheduled classroom observation cannot reveal a teacher's trade-off patterns because those patterns only become visible through repetition -- across sections, across days, between a plan and its execution.

Applying Smith and Lewis's paradox theory, the piece distinguishes a dilemma (a one-time choice you settle) from a paradox (two permanently competing demands, like participation and order, that must be managed continuously rather than resolved).

Poole and Van de Ven's four responses to an unresolvable paradox -- separation by space, separation by time, synthesis, and acceptance -- give coaches a vocabulary for naming what a teacher is actually doing rather than just praising or critiquing the outcome.

The student teacher's shift between a tight 3rd period and a loose 4th period looks like a deliberate "separation by space" strategy but is actually an unnamed reaction, illustrating that the difference between a coping move and an accident is whether the teacher can name what they are doing and why.

The author's coaching "talk move" reframes feedback around naming the competing demand being served ("you cut that question short to protect pacing -- what did that cost you?") rather than evaluating whether the outcome was good or bad.
quotes: I've come to realize how little I'd actually seen of her teaching last spring, even working three feet away the whole time. Watching someone assist isn't the same as watching someone decide.

In 3rd period she runs a tight, structured discussion - clear turns, every voice accountable. In 4th, same lesson, the room gets looser. More crosstalk, more energy, less control. I used to call that inconsistency. It's not.

Wendy Smith and Marianne Lewis make a distinction I now use: a dilemma is a one-time choice you weigh and settle. A paradox is different - two demands that are both true, both necessary, and permanently in tension, where pushing on one makes the other louder.
My student teacher has been doing none of these on purpose. What she's been doing looks like separation by space - tight in 3rd, loose in 4th - but it isn't a strategy. It's a reaction.

That's the case I'm now making to other coaches: do your office time inside classrooms, not down the hall. Not for visibility and not because more data is automatically better, but because a coach who sees the same teacher's two sections is positioned to notice whether the cycling between poles is deliberate or accidental.
Instead: "You cut that question short to protect the pacing. What did that cost you - and in 4th, when you let it run, was that a choice or did it just happen to you?
